subject: A theoretical question on bifactor models

messages.author: 4b06c0bae2d1991d
messages.subject: A theoretical question on bifactor models
parts:
I realize the utility of bifactor models. However, how can the specific factors be interpreted if they are orthogonal from each other and from the general factor? It makes sense in educational/intelligence testing, but not in psychopathology.

For example: there is a long history in aggression research to separate reactive aggression (being provoked) from proactive aggression (starting fights). Most scales create 2 highly correlated factors. But there is strong evidence for unidimensionality (e.g. in one scale, the first to second eigenvalue ratio is 11:1). That makes sense - all items measure aggression. Its a great place for a bifactor model with aggression as the general factor and specific factors of reactivity/proactivity.

But how is it logical to discuss reactive (aggression) uncorrelated with general aggression? Is that even a fair question?

I know this isn't a question about the mirt package, but you said this group can discuss IRT questions in general, and so I give a theoretical one. I appreciate any interpretations you can offer.

Thanks!
Aaron

I'm not sure that bifactor is more appropriate than a 2 general
dimension model. I reach for bifactor when there are otherwise too many
general dimensions to practically fit.

> But how is it logical to discuss reactive (aggression) uncorrelated
> with general aggression? Is that even a fair question?

Factors are orthogonal when fitting for technical reasons, but that
doesn't mean you shouldn't do an oblique rotation like promax. You
should!

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: A theoretical question on bifactor models
parts:
On Sat, May 11, 2013 at 2:16 PM, <aaron...@gmail.com> wrote:
I realize the utility of bifactor models. However, how can the specific factors be interpreted if they are orthogonal from each other and from the general factor? It makes sense in educational/intelligence testing, but not in psychopathology.

For example: there is a long history in aggression research to separate reactive aggression (being provoked) from proactive aggression (starting fights).  Most scales create 2 highly correlated factors. But there is strong evidence for unidimensionality (e.g. in one scale, the first to second eigenvalue ratio is 11:1). That makes sense - all items measure aggression.  Its a great place for a bifactor model with aggression as the general factor and specific factors of reactivity/proactivity.

Well, to start on the interpretation looking at the specific factors must be interpreted with respect to the general construct, and as such the specific factor coefficient are 'partial' effects after holding the general construct constant. So in that sense interpreting 'reactive aggression' after the 'general aggression' commonality has been removed gives a kind of 'reactive only' construct which is independent of general aggression. I think it's up to the researcher whether this kind of quasi-purified specific factor is of any practical utility. 

Most times in educational/intelligence testing specific factors have been treated only as nuance item blocks that aren't of much theoretical interest but must be accounted for due to similar content (or whatever) presented that creates unwanted inter-item dependencies. I think the philosophy of a bifactor model is that whenever you want to create a composite score to best measure your unidimensional construct, but due to known limitations in testing that cause interdependency blocks you want to try to minimize these effects as much as possible to make the measurement of your construct as pure as possible. 

That being said, in your example there are probably two such approaches that are research dependent. If you are interested in a kind of general aggression effect, then I don't see much problem in using a bifactor model and focusing on the general factor, but if you are more interested in how proactive and reactive aggression differ in empirical settings then keeping them separate would probably be more suitable. Notice that these are just two different emphases and your research interests largely determine the kind of route to take.

Also note: a large eigenvalue drop is not strictly indicative of undimensionality, but certainly can indicate highly correlating factors. It may require adding additional items to help detect the subtle differences between the related constructs and validate the constructs by correlating them with externally meaningful criteria.

But how is it logical to discuss reactive (aggression) uncorrelated with general aggression? Is that even a fair question?

I know this isn't a question about the mirt package, but you said this group can discuss IRT questions in general, and so I give a theoretical one.  I appreciate any interpretations you can offer.
Feel free to ask away, I've just been replying to a lot of emails about practical and theoretical IRT stuff and figured making them public might help others in the future. Cheers.

messages.author: 4b06c0bae2d1991d
messages.subject: Re: A theoretical question on bifactor models
parts:
This is a reply to both of you - thank you for your responses:

First, to Joshua, I disagree that the bifactor should be used only when "there are otherwise too many dimensions" - with MCMC or partial MCMC methods (e.g. MH-RM), high dimensionality is less of a concern than in the past. The advantage of the bifactor is that it allows an interpretative total score, something that most tests use (e.g. total anxiety, total aggression, IQ). And of course, when not using the bifactor model I favor oblique rotations (though my preference is for direct oblimin - promax rotates to an orthogonal prior to the oblique rotation and I dislike that).

Second, to both of you, the problem is wanting both an interpretive total score AND subscales. It is very common to want total aggression and reactive/proactive subscales (using my prior example), or total anxiety and separation/generalized/social/panic disorder subscales. To use correlated general factors works, but then a simple sum score for the total score isn't based on the data; its because we want it. A second-order factor could be used, but then that is based off of the latent factor correlations and not the manifest data (and for 2 subscales, like my aggression example, would need to have additional restrictions to be identified).

The problem, then, is how to choose which model is best. Correlated factors are at least nested within the second-order model, so a chi-square difference test is possible. But the bifactor model stands apart - only AIC/BIC comparisons are possible. Is that enough evidence to favor the bifactor over the correlated factors, or vice versa. In reality, I want both: I want a meaningful total score and meaningful subscales.

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: A theoretical question on bifactor models
parts: On Mon, May 13, 2013 at 11:43 AM, <aaron...@gmail.com> wrote:

This is a reply to both of you - thank you for your responses:

First, to Joshua, I disagree that the bifactor should be used only when "there are otherwise too many dimensions" - with MCMC or partial MCMC methods (e.g. MH-RM), high dimensionality is less of a concern than in the past. The advantage of the bifactor is that it allows an interpretative total score, something that most tests use (e.g. total anxiety, total aggression, IQ). And of course, when not using the bifactor model I favor oblique rotations (though my preference is for direct oblimin - promax rotates to an orthogonal prior to the oblique rotation and I dislike that).

Second, to both of you, the problem is wanting both an interpretive total score AND subscales.  It is very common to want total aggression and reactive/proactive subscales (using my prior example), or total anxiety and separation/generalized/social/panic disorder subscales.

But are these not different research questions and as such suggest different methods for analysis? They are different constructs after all and can refer to very different empirical phenomenon. One could make the same argument when studying a math test: is general understanding of math of interest, or are we more interested in analyzing only the 'addition' components and how they relate to 'multiplication'. In the former a bifactor analysis seems reasonable, while in the latter it doesn't (unless the question is addition and multiplication after general math ability has been accounted for....).

To use correlated general factors works, but then a simple sum score for the total score isn't based on the data; its because we want it.  A second-order factor could be used, but then that is based off of the latent factor correlations and not the manifest data (and for 2 subscales, like my aggression example, would need to have additional restrictions to be identified).

If you want to create a composite that is formed from all the common variance between each variable, regardless of underlying structure (since the specific factors are not the interesting phenomenon), then a bifactor model is a reasonable approach. If on the other-hand the composite should be taken as the sum of the specific components that comprise the tests components then a higher-order factor analysis would seem more reasonable. 

Going back to your example the question is then which would fit into the research paradigm of aggression: is aggression the primary phenomenon that manifests itself in different ways (proactive, reactive, etc) that aren't all that important for the research question at hand or fundamentally defined by said behavior, or is aggression the sum of it's specific factor manifestations (aggression is defined by proactive, reactive, etc, tendencies)? They have subtle but important implications for therapy, since if the treatment is geared towards only reducing 'reactive aggression' then according to the bifactor model the general aggression construct may be unaffected by the change in this behavior (aggressive people just don't react to events as much, but still remain highly aggressive), while in the second-order model reducing reactive aggression behavior would reduce the overall aggression composite. Again, this is a domain and application specific problem, and since I don't have any experience in this particular research I can't offer a solution. 

The meaningfulness of the composite score (whether you go with a bifactor or higher-order) is determined by what the specific factors really represent and how important the general factor is to the research paradigm. If interpreting the raw coefficients is important for the specific factors then a second-order model would probably be easier.

The problem, then, is how to choose which model is best.  Correlated factors are at least nested within the second-order model, so a chi-square difference test is possible. But the bifactor model stands apart - only AIC/BIC comparisons are possible.  Is that enough evidence to favor the bifactor over the correlated factors, or vice versa.  In reality, I want both: I want a meaningful total score and meaningful subscales.
